claim: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a worldwide health issue, representing a heterogeneous and aggressive disease with the leading cause of tumor-associated lethality.
source: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a worldwide health issue, representing a heterogeneous and aggressive disease with the leading cause of tumor-associated lethality (Sung et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sung et al., 2021

claim: Pathological staging is broadly but inadequately used to guide clinical management due to diverse clinical outcomes of patients within the same stage.
source: Currently, pathological staging is broadly but inadequately used to guide clinical management due to diverse clinical outcomes of patients within the same stage (Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2022

claim: The inherent heterogeneity between patients hampers the individualized treatment of CRC.
source: The inherent heterogeneity between patients hampers the individualized treatment of CRC.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about cancer heterogeneity and treatment challenges

claim: Development of molecular classification takes the plunge toward more effective interventions and provides critical insights into CRC heterogeneity.
source: Development of molecular classification takes the plunge toward more effective interventions and provides critical insights into CRC heterogeneity (Guinney et al., 2015; Isella et al., 2017; De Sousa E Melo et al., 2013; Sadanandam et al., 2013; Marisa et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous molecular classification studies

claim: Molecular subtypes with distinctive peculiarities and outcomes are mainly identified based on the snapshot transcriptional profiles, largely ignoring the dynamic changes of gene expressions in a biological system.
source: However, molecular subtypes with distinctive peculiarities and outcoms are mainly identified based on the snapshot transcriptional profiles, largely ignoring the dynamic changes of gene expressions in a biological system (Guinney et al., 2015 ; Isella et al., 2017; De Sousa E Melo et al., 2013; Sadanandam et al., 2013; Marisa et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2021a).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous classification studies and Chen et al., 2021a

claim: Gene expressions are commonly variable at distinct time points or conditions, so that the subtypes based on expression data are unstable and difficult to reproduce.
source: Indeed, gene expressions are commonly variable at distinct time points or conditions, so that the subtypes based on expression data are unstable and difficult to reproduce (Chen et al., 2021b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2021b

claim: Biological networks remain relatively stable irrespective of time and condition, and could more reliably characterize the biological state of bulk tissues.
source: Conversely, biological networks remain relatively stable irrespective of time and condition, and could more reliably characterize the biological state of bulk tissues (Chen et al., 2021a; Sahni et al., 2015; Li et al., 2019a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2021a; Sahni et al., 2015; Li et al., 2019a

claim: Network analysis is well documented and applied in high-dimensional data, performing more robustly and effectively than single-gene approach.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that network analysis is well documented and applied in high-dimensional data, performing more robustly and effectively than single-gene approach (Chen et al., 2021b; Sahni et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2021b; Sahni et al., 2015

claim: Most network-based methods merely focus on gene nodes in the biological network, but ignore the interactions among genes.
source: Nevertheless, most network-based methods merely focus on gene nodes in the biological network, but ignore the interactions among genes.
evidence: Based on inference from the literature review and motivation for the study

claim: Gene interactions are highly conservative in normal samples but broadly perturbed in diseased tissues.
source: Gene interactions are highly conservative in normal samples but broadly perturbed in diseased tissues (Sahni et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sahni et al., 2015

claim: The interaction perturbation within the network can quantify the interaction change for each gene pair.
source: The interaction perturbation within the network can quantify the interaction change for each gene pair.
evidence: Based on the methodological approach described

claim: The overall perturbation of all gene pairs in the background network is reasonably and effectively utilized to characterize the pathological condition at the individual level.
source: Thus, the overall perturbation of all gene pairs in the background network is reasonably and effectively utilized to characterize the pathological condition at the individual level.
evidence: Based on the methodological rationale

claim: Six gene interaction network-based subtypes (GINS1-6) were identified with distinct clinical and molecular peculiarities.
source: Using the individual-specific gene interaction perturbation network-based program, we identified and diversely validated six gene interaction network-based subtypes (GINS1-6) with distinct clinical and molecular peculiarities.
evidence: Primary finding of the study, supported by data presented in the manuscript

claim: The results provided a high-resolution classification system and improved the understanding of CRC heterogeneity from an interactome perspective.
source: Our results provided a high-resolution classification system and improved the understanding of CRC heterogeneity from an interactome perspective.
evidence: Conclusion based on the study findings

claim: A network with 1390 genes and 2225 interactions was formed for clustering analysis.
source: To decipher the heterogeneous subtypes from the interaction-perturbation matrix (Materials and methods, Figure 1), we selected the representative features that significantly distinguished tumor from normal samples and maintained high variability within all tumor samples for clustering analysis, which formed a network with 1390 genes and 2225 interactions.
evidence: Methodological detail supported by data

claim: The new network met the scale-free distribution (R=−0.994, p<2.2e-16).
source: This new network also met the scale-free distribution (R=−0.994, p<2.2e-16; Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) and was visualized in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figure reference

claim: Consensus clustering analysis on the discovery cohort with 2,167 CRC samples and 2,225 gene interactions initially tested potential clustering numbers (K=2–10).
source: Consensus clustering analysis (Wilkerson and Hayes, 2010) on the discovery cohort with 2,167 CRC samples and 2,225 gene interactions, initially tested potential clustering numbers (K=2–10).
evidence: Methodological detail with citation

claim: The cumulative distribution function (CDF) curve and the proportion of ambiguous clustering (PAC) score suggested the optimal K=6.
source: The cumulative distribution function (CDF) curve and the proportion of ambiguous clustering (PAC) score (Senbabaoğlu et al., 2014) of the consensus score matrix suggested the optimal K=6, which was also achieved from the Nbclust assessment (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis, citation, and figure references

claim: The silhouette statistic yielded a core set of 1957 CRC samples.
source: The silhouette statistic was utilized to identify the samples that best represented one of six gene interaction-perturbation network subtypes (GINS), yielding a core set of 1957 CRC samples (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figure reference

claim: The Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) showed good discrimination among the six subtypes.
source: The Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP)(Becht et al., 2019) cast all samples in two-dimensional spatial coordinates, showing good discrimination (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by visualization method citation and figure reference

claim: Age and gender did not differ in distribution among the six subtypes (p>0.05).
source: In the six subtypes, age and gender did not differ in distribution (p>0.05; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-B), whereas the clinicopathological stage was more advanced in GINS2 than the other subtypes (p<0.05; Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-F).
evidence: Supported by statistical test and figure reference

claim: The clinicopathological stage was more advanced in GINS2 than the other subtypes (p<0.05).
source: In the six subtypes, age and gender did not differ in distribution (p>0.05; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-B), whereas the clinicopathological stage was more advanced in GINS2 than the other subtypes (p<0.05; Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-F).
evidence: Supported by statistical test and figure reference

claim: Microsatellite instability (MSI) was prominently enriched in GINS5 (p<2.2e-16).
source: Microsatellite instability (MSI), a well-established biomarker in CRC (Raskov et al., 2020), was prominently enriched in GINS5 (p<2.2e-16; Figure 2—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: Supported by statistical test, citation, and figure reference

claim: GINS2 had the worst prognostic outcomes of overall survival (OS) and relapse-free survival (RFS).
source: Kaplan-Meier survival analysis demonstrated significant survival differences among six subtypes. GINS2 had the worst prognostic outcomes of overall survival (OS) and relapse-free survival (RFS), whereas GINS5 portended the most favorable prognosis, and the other four subtypes displayed intermedium OS and RFS (OS, p<0.0001; RFS, p<0.0001; Figure 2C–D).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier analysis and figure reference

claim: GINS5 portended the most favorable prognosis.
source: Kaplan-Meier survival analysis demonstrated significant survival differences among six subtypes. GINS2 had the worst prognostic outcomes of overall survival (OS) and relapse-free survival (RFS), whereas GINS5 portended the most favorable prognosis, and the other four subtypes displayed intermedium OS and RFS (OS, p<0.0001; RFS, p<0.0001; Figure 2C–D).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier analysis and figure reference

claim: GINS2 benefited more from fluorouracil-based adjuvant chemotherapy in the discovery cohort with 79 responders and 187 non-responders (p=2.67e-5).
source: Additionally, GINS2 benefited more from fluorouracil-based adjuvant chemotherapy (ACT) in the discovery cohort with 79 responders and 187 non-responders (p=2.67e-5, Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by statistical test and figure reference

claim: Only GINS2 tumors had significantly improved survival after ACT treatment.
source: Subsequent analysis focused on each subtype and revealed that only GINS2 tumors had significantly improved survival after ACT treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B-G), suggesting these patients were preferentially responsive to ACT.
evidence: Supported by survival analysis and figure reference

claim: GINS2 might benefit less from bevacizumab in the discovery cohort (25 responders and 29 non-responders), whereas GINS3 possessed a large proportion of responders (p=0.042).
source: Conversely, GINS2 might benefit less from bevacizumab in the discovery cohort (25 responders and 29 non-responders), whereas GINS3 possessed a large proportion of responders (p=0.042; Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by statistical test and figure reference

claim: Noteworthy connections were observed between GINS subtypes and previous CRC classifications, indicating a biological convergence.
source: Noteworthy connections were observed between our subtypes and these previous classifications, indicating a biological convergence (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by comparison analysis and figure reference

claim: GINS1 was related to the canonical CMS2, CCS1, CRCA5, and CIT1.
source: Specifically, GINS1 was related to the canonical CMS2, CCS1, CRCA5, and CIT1; GINS2 was associated with the more aggressive subtypes, including CMS4, CRIS-B, CCS3, CRCA3, and CIT5; GINS3 was linked to CMS2, CRIS-C, CCS1, CRCA2/5, and CIT1; GINS4 was correlated with CMS4, CRIS-A, CCS1/3, and CRCA3; GINS5 was predominantly enriched in MSI-like subtypes, containing CMS1, CRIS-A, CCS2, CRCA4, and CIT2; GINS6 was associated with CMS3, CRIS-A, CCS3, CRCA1, and CIT6.
evidence: Supported by comparison with previous classification systems

claim: GINS2 was associated with the more aggressive subtypes, including CMS4, CRIS-B, CCS3, CRCA3, and CIT5.
source: Specifically, GINS1 was related to the canonical CMS2, CCS1, CRCA5, and CIT1; GINS2 was associated with the more aggressive subtypes, including CMS4, CRIS-B, CCS3, CRCA3, and CIT5; GINS3 was linked to CMS2, CRIS-C, CCS1, CRCA2/5, and CIT1; GINS4 was correlated with CMS4, CRIS-A, CCS1/3, and CRCA3; GINS5 was predominantly enriched in MSI-like subtypes, containing CMS1, CRIS-A, CCS2, CRCA4, and CIT2; GINS6 was associated with CMS3, CRIS-A, CCS3, CRCA1, and CIT6.
evidence: Supported by comparison with previous classification systems

claim: Only approximately 50% of the classifier genes overlapped with the signature genes of all previous CRC classifications.
source: Notably, only approximately 50% of our classifier genes overlapped with the signature genes of all previous CRC classifications (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), suggesting a significant molecular convergence, but also leaving a rich exploration space for our classification.
evidence: Supported by overlap analysis and figure reference

claim: A 289-gene centroid-based classifier was developed with the lowest misclassification error (1.8%).
source: We first identified genes correlated with the six subtypes using significance analysis of microarrays (Tusher et al., 2001), followed by prediction analysis for microarrays (Tibshirani et al., 2002) to determine 289 subtype-discriminant genes with the lowest misclassification error (1.8%) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and citations

claim: Six subtypes were confidently identified in seven datasets from the same platform, and SubMap analysis confirmed that each subtype was associated with similar underlying transcriptional traits in the discovery cohort.
source: Initially, significant subtype assignments were performed on seven datasets from the same platform via the 289-gene centroid-based classifier (Supplementary file 16). Six subtypes were confidently identified, and Subclass Mapping (SubMap) analysis (Hoshida et al., 2007) confirmed that each subtype was associated with similar underlying transcriptional traits in the discovery cohort (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by SubMap analysis, citation, and figure reference

claim: The same results were achieved on seven microarrays from different platforms and one RNA-seq dataset (TCGA-CRC Illumina).
source: The same results were achieved on seven microarrays from different platforms and one RNA-seq dataset (TCGA-CRC Illumina; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by validation across different platforms and figure reference

claim: Analysis using datasets containing samples from both microdissected and whole tumors consistently reproduced six subtypes with particular molecular traits.
source: To address this issue, our analysis using additional datasets (GSE12945 and GSE21510) containing samples from both microdissected and whole tumors, and from tumor RNAs profiled on different microarray platforms, consistently reproduced six subtypes with particular molecular traits (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: Supported by analysis of microdissected and whole tumor samples and figure reference

claim: Comparable fractions of patients were assigned to each subtype in the discovery cohort and 19 validation datasets.
source: In the discovery cohort and 19 validation datasets, we found comparable fractions of patients being assigned to each subtype (Figure 3C), which demonstrated that our classification was stable and universal within different datasets.
evidence: Supported by comparison across datasets and figure reference

claim: GINS2 possessed more advanced tumors in validation datasets.
source: Likewise, GINS2 possessed more advanced tumors (Supplementary file 2), preferentially metastasized (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A-F), and behaved adverse OS (Figure 3D–H) and RFS (Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 4G-H).
evidence: Supported by clinical data analysis and figure references

claim: The MSI tumors were prone to occur in GINS5 in validation datasets.
source: The MSI tumors were prone to occur in GINS5 (Figure 3J–P) with the most favorable OS (Figure 3D–H) and RFS (Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 4G-H).
evidence: Supported by MSI distribution analysis and figure references

claim: ACT treatment exhibited the identical response distribution, with GINS2 achieving more clinical benefit in validation datasets.
source: ACT treatment also exhibited the identical response distribution, with GINS2 achieving more clinical benefit (Figure 3Q).
evidence: Supported by treatment response analysis and figure reference

claim: Cetuximab performed better in GINS3.
source: Cetuximab with function to target EGFR (Raskov et al., 2020), performed better in GINS3 (Figure 3R).
evidence: Supported by treatment response analysis, citation, and figure reference

claim: A 14-gene miniclassifier was developed using LASSO framework and random forest model.
source: Subsequently, the LASSO framework based on 10-fold cross-validation and one-standard-error rule determined the 14 most informative genes that integratively fitted a random forest model (Figure 4A and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by machine learning methodology and figure reference

claim: The random forest model had a misclassification error of 7.8% in the training dataset and 13.0% in the testing dataset.
source: Confusion matrix displayed the general tendency of classification effect, with a misclassification error of 7.8% and 13.0% in the training and testing datasets, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: Supported by model performance evaluation and figure reference

claim: The miniclassifier successfully isolated six subtypes in 214 frozen CRC tissues validated by qPCR.
source: To test the clinical interpretation of this miniclassifier, another validation based on qPCR results from 214 frozen CRC tissues was deployed to verify its feasibility in clinical settings. With the expression profiles of 14 key genes in each patient, the miniclassifier successfully isolated six subtypes (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by qPCR validation in clinical samples

claim: In the clinical validation cohort, GINS2 had shorter OS and RFS (p<0.0001).
source: In line with our prior findings, GINS2 had shorter OS and RFS (p<0.0001, Figure 4C–D), behaved a stronger propensity to invade and metastasize (p=0.002, Figure 4E and Supplementary file 5), but was sensitive to ACT treatment (p=0.041, Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by survival analysis in clinical cohort and figure references

claim: GINS1 was distinguished by up-regulated cell cycle pathways, suggesting proliferative characteristics.
source: According to the SSEA and GSVA phenotypic analysis, GINS1 was distinguished by up-regulated cell cycle pathways, suggesting proliferative characteristics for these tumors (Figure 5A–B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 7).
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis and figure references

claim: GINS1 strikingly overexpressed MKI67 and PCNA (p<2.2e-16).
source: We next proved that GINS1 also strikingly overexpressed MKI67 and PCNA (p<2.2e-16, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-B), which were identified as important cell cycle-specific antigens in tumors.
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis and figure reference

claim: GINS3 exhibited an inferior level of KRAS signaling that was mainly driven by KRAS mutations.
source: GINS3 exhibited an inferior level of KRAS signaling that was mainly driven by KRAS mutations (Figure 5A–B and Supplementary file 7; Raskov et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis, figure reference, and citation

claim: Activation of metabolisms (mainly lipid metabolisms) was featured by GINS6, suggesting canonical metabolic reprogramming.
source: Activation of metabolisms (mainly lipid metabolisms) was featured by GINS6, suggesting canonical metabolic reprogramming across these tumors (Figure 5A–B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 7).
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis and figure references

claim: GINS2 was endowed with higher stromal activity and lower immune activity.
source: Intriguingly, interactive stromal and immune activation trends shifted in GINS2/4/5 (Figure 5A–B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 7). GINS2 was endowed with higher stromal activity and lower immune activity, whereas GINS5 conveyed the opposite trend entirely, concordant with the tumor invasiveness and prognosis of two subtypes, and GINS4 was characterized by a mixed phenotype that displayed moderate level of stromal and immune pathways.
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis and figure references

claim: GINS5 conveyed higher immune activity and lower stromal activity.
source: Intriguingly, interactive stromal and immune activation trends shifted in GINS2/4/5 (Figure 5A–B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 7). GINS2 was endowed with higher stromal activity and lower immune activity, whereas GINS5 conveyed the opposite trend entirely, concordant with the tumor invasiveness and prognosis of two subtypes, and GINS4 was characterized by a mixed phenotype that displayed moderate level of stromal and immune pathways.
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis and figure references

claim: GINS4 was characterized by a mixed phenotype that displayed moderate level of stromal and immune pathways.
source: Intriguingly, interactive stromal and immune activation trends shifted in GINS2/4/5 (Figure 5A–B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 7). GINS2 was endowed with higher stromal activity and lower immune activity, whereas GINS5 conveyed the opposite trend entirely, concordant with the tumor invasiveness and prognosis of two subtypes, and GINS4 was characterized by a mixed phenotype that displayed moderate level of stromal and immune pathways.
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis and figure references

claim: ESTIMATE further validated the stromal and immune differences among GINS2/4/5 (p<2.2e-16).
source: ESTIMATE (Yoshihara et al., 2013), a tool that uses gene expression profiles to infer immune and stromal constituents within the tumor microenvironment (TME), further validated these phenomena (p<2.2e-16, Figure 5—figure supplement 2C-D).
evidence: Supported by ESTIMATE analysis, citation, and figure reference

claim: Gene cluster 3 was prevailingly associated with immune infiltration and activation.
source: As expected, gene cluster 3 was prevailingly associated with immune infiltration and activation (Figure 5D), whereas gene cluster 10 was prominently characterized by stromal activation and remodeling (Figure 5E), which further supported our findings.
evidence: Supported by gene cluster enrichment analysis and figure reference

claim: Gene cluster 10 was prominently characterized by stromal activation and remodeling.
source: As expected, gene cluster 3 was prevailingly associated with immune infiltration and activation (Figure 5D), whereas gene cluster 10 was prominently characterized by stromal activation and remodeling (Figure 5E), which further supported our findings.
evidence: Supported by gene cluster enrichment analysis and figure reference

claim: GINS1/3 displayed scarce stromal and immune components and possessed higher tumor purity.
source: Of note, GINS1/3 displayed scarce stromal and immune components (Figure 5A–B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C-D), instead, tumors within these subtypes possessed higher purity (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by TME analysis and figure references

claim: Tumors with high expression pattern of immunomodulators were predominantly assigned to GINS5.
source: Our results delineated that transcriptional expression of immunomodulators varied across GINS subtypes, and tumors with high expression pattern of immunomodulators were predominantly assigned to GINS5 (Figure 6A and Supplementary file 9).
evidence: Supported by immunomodulator expression analysis and figure reference

claim: 13/26 of immunomodulators were up-regulated in GINS5 at protein level.
source: Differential analysis with the thresholds of Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate <0.05 and log2 (fold change)>1 was performed between GINS5 and other subtypes, and we observed 13/26 of immunomodulators were up-regulated in GINS5 (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by proteome data analysis and figure reference

claim: 12/13 of significant immunomodulators are involved in antigen presentation.
source: More specifically, 12/13 of significant immunomodulators are involved in antigen presentation, another protein was IDO1, an emerging immune checkpoint that overexpresses in multiple cancers (Zhai et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by functional annotation and citation

claim: GINS5 was characterized by remarkably higher tumor mutation burden (TMB) and neoantigen load (NAL) (p<0.001).
source: GINS5 was also characterized by a stronger immunogenicity that harbored remarkably higher tumor mutation burden (TMB) and neoantigen load (NAL) (p<0.001, Figure 6C), possibly further inducing abundant immune elements and regulations.
evidence: Supported by TMB and NAL analysis and figure reference

claim: Rich infiltration and strong immune killing of T cells were particularly evident in GINS5.
source: Using these tools, we found that rich infiltration and strong immune killing of T cells were particularly evident in GINS5, coincident with the abovementioned findings (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by immune cell infiltration analysis and figure reference

claim: GINS5 possessed the abundant infiltration of Th1, Th2, and M1 macrophages.
source: Moreover, GINS5 also possessed the abundant infiltration of Th1, Th2, and M1 macrophages (Mills et al., 2016; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-C), which could secrete proinflammatory cytokines and enhance immune activation.
evidence: Supported by immune cell infiltration analysis, citation, and figure reference

claim: M2 macrophages were significantly elevated in GINS2.
source: Conversely, M2 traditionally regarded as promoting tumor growth by suppressing cell-mediated immunity and subsequent cancer cell killing (Mills et al., 2016), was significantly elevated in GINS2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by immune cell infiltration analysis, citation, and figure reference

claim: Fibroblasts, myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSC), and Treg cells were significantly enriched in GINS2.
source: In line with this, three other classical immunosuppressive cells, including fibroblasts, myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSC), and Treg cells (Hicks et al., 2022), were also significantly enriched in GINS2 (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by immune cell infiltration analysis, citation, and figure reference

claim: GINS1/3 displayed sparse infiltration of cells that promote immune activity.
source: Apart from the immune activation represented by GINS5, GINS1/2/3 displayed sparse infiltration of cells that promote immune activity (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-C), but unlike GINS2, GINS1/3 were also characterized by rare immunosuppressive cells (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), consistent with their high tumor purity.
evidence: Supported by immune cell infiltration analysis and figure references

claim: GINS1/3 were characterized by rare immunosuppressive cells, consistent with their high tumor purity.
source: Apart from the immune activation represented by GINS5, GINS1/2/3 displayed sparse infiltration of cells that promote immune activity (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-C), but unlike GINS2, GINS1/3 were also characterized by rare immunosuppressive cells (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), consistent with their high tumor purity.
evidence: Supported by immune cell infiltration analysis and figure references

claim: GINS1/3 were designated the 'immune-desert' phenotype.
source: Together, we annotated six subtypes by specific immune features: (i) GINS1/3, thereafter designated the 'immune-desert' phenotype, was endowed with scarce immune fractions; (ii) GINS2, thereafter designated the 'immune-suppressed' phenotype, was enriched for abundant inhibitory cells; (iii) GINS5, thereafter designated the 'immune-activated' phenotype, was dramatically linked to superior tumor immunogenicity and extensive immune activation; and (iv) GINS4/6, thereafter designated the 'mixed' phenotype, was characterized by moderate levels of immunity cycle score (Figure 6F).
evidence: Based on immune profiling analysis and figure reference

claim: GINS2 was designated the 'immune-suppressed' phenotype.
source: Together, we annotated six subtypes by specific immune features: (i) GINS1/3, thereafter designated the 'immune-desert' phenotype, was endowed with scarce immune fractions; (ii) GINS2, thereafter designated the 'immune-suppressed' phenotype, was enriched for abundant inhibitory cells; (iii) GINS5, thereafter designated the 'immune-activated' phenotype, was dramatically linked to superior tumor immunogenicity and extensive immune activation; and (iv) GINS4/6, thereafter designated the 'mixed' phenotype, was characterized by moderate levels of immunity cycle score (Figure 6F).
evidence: Based on immune profiling analysis and figure reference

claim: GINS5 was designated the 'immune-activated' phenotype.
source: Together, we annotated six subtypes by specific immune features: (i) GINS1/3, thereafter designated the 'immune-desert' phenotype, was endowed with scarce immune fractions; (ii) GINS2, thereafter designated the 'immune-suppressed' phenotype, was enriched for abundant inhibitory cells; (iii) GINS5, thereafter designated the 'immune-activated' phenotype, was dramatically linked to superior tumor immunogenicity and extensive immune activation; and (iv) GINS4/6, thereafter designated the 'mixed' phenotype, was characterized by moderate levels of immunity cycle score (Figure 6F).
evidence: Based on immune profiling analysis and figure reference

claim: GINS4/6 were designated the 'mixed' phenotype.
source: Together, we annotated six subtypes by specific immune features: (i) GINS1/3, thereafter designated the 'immune-desert' phenotype, was endowed with scarce immune fractions; (ii) GINS2, thereafter designated the 'immune-suppressed' phenotype, was enriched for abundant inhibitory cells; (iii) GINS5, thereafter designated the 'immune-activated' phenotype, was dramatically linked to superior tumor immunogenicity and extensive immune activation; and (iv) GINS4/6, thereafter designated the 'mixed' phenotype, was characterized by moderate levels of immunity cycle score (Figure 6F).
evidence: Based on immune profiling analysis and figure reference

claim: Patients with lower TIDE score, higher immunophenoscore and T-cell-inflamed gene expression profiles were predominantly assigned to GINS5.
source: Among these six subtypes, patients with lower tumor immune dysfunction and exclusion score (Jiang et al., 2018), higher immunophenoscore (Charoentong et al., 2017) and T-cell-inflamed gene expression profiles (Ott et al., 2019), were proven to favor benefit from immunotherapy, and predominantly assigned to GINS5 (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by immunotherapy biomarker analysis, citations, and figure reference

claim: SubMap analysis delineated the similar expression pattern between GISN5 tumors and immunotherapeutic responders from three cohorts.
source: SubMap analysis (Hoshida et al., 2007) also delineated the similar expression pattern between GISN5 tumors and immunotherapeutic responders from three cohorts with treatment annotations, and GINS1/2/3 shared the transcriptional modes with non-responders from 2/3 of immunotherapeutic cohorts (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by SubMap analysis, citation, and figure reference

claim: GINS1/2/3 shared the transcriptional modes with non-responders from 2/3 of immunotherapeutic cohorts.
source: SubMap analysis (Hoshida et al., 2007) also delineated the similar expression pattern between GISN5 tumors and immunotherapeutic responders from three cohorts with treatment annotations, and GINS1/2/3 shared the transcriptional modes with non-responders from 2/3 of immunotherapeutic cohorts (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by SubMap analysis, citation, and figure reference

claim: 20 metabolic pathways were significantly enriched in GINS6 versus other subtypes, and most pathways were upregulated.
source: In total, 20 pathways were significantly enriched in GINS6 versus other subtypes, and most pathways were upregulated (Figure 7A and Supplementary file 11).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis and figure reference

claim: Lipid metabolisms were the most significant metabolic processes in GINS6.
source: Notably, GSEA demonstrated that lipid metabolisms were the most significant metabolic processes in GINS6 (Figure 7A–B and Supplementary file 11).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis and figure reference

claim: Only the lipid metabolism profiles could distinguish GINS6 from other subtypes in spatial distribution using PCA.
source: Using principal component analysis (PCA), we found that only the lipid metabolism profiles could distinguish GINS6 from other subtypes in spatial distribution (Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis and figure reference

claim: GINS6 predominantly enriched high-ranking samples with stronger lipid signature scores.
source: The SSEA-based framework further confirmed that GINS6 predominantly enriched high-ranking samples with stronger lipid signature scores (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by SSEA analysis and figure reference

claim: 7/9 of GINS6-specific genes belonged to lipid metabolic pathways.
source: Subsequently, we established a metabolite-protein interaction network (MPIN)(Chen et al., 2021a) via nine GINS6-specific genes with broad and tight connections with lipid metabolites (Figure 7E and Supplementary file 12). Indeed, 7/9 of these genes belonged to lipid metabolic pathways.
evidence: Supported by MPIN analysis, citation, and figure reference

claim: GINS6 exhibited higher levels in four fatty acids including α-glycerophosphate, adipate, taurocholate, and aconitate.
source: We compared the metabolite abundances between GINS6 and other subtypes, and found that GINS6 exhibited higher levels in four fatty acids including α-glycerophosphate, adipate, taurocholate, and aconitate.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics analysis in cell lines

claim: Four carnitines containing stearoylcarnitine, myristoylcarnitine, valerylcarnitine, and malonylcarnitine were dramatically accumulated in GINS6.
source: Additionally, four carnitines containing stearoylcarnitine, myristoylcarnitine, valerylcarnitine, and malonylcarnitine, that serve as vital compounds in lipid metabolism processes, were also dramatically accumulated in GINS6 (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics analysis and figure reference

claim: GINS2 appeared highly enriched for stem-cell-like tumors (91%).
source: In this study, GINS2 appeared highly enriched for stem-cell-like tumors (91%), whereas GINS4 was endowed with transit-amplifying-like phenotype (86%) (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by cellular phenotype analysis and figure reference

claim: GINS4 was endowed with transit-amplifying-like phenotype (86%).
source: In this study, GINS2 appeared highly enriched for stem-cell-like tumors (91%), whereas GINS4 was endowed with transit-amplifying-like phenotype (86%) (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by cellular phenotype analysis and figure reference

claim: GINS5 was characterized by inflammatory phenotype.
source: GINS5 was characterized by inflammatory (Figure 8A), coincident with its biological and immune features.
evidence: Supported by cellular phenotype analysis and figure reference

claim: GINS6 featured an enterocyte-like phenotype.
source: GINS6 featured an enterocyte-like phenotype (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by cellular phenotype analysis and figure reference

claim: Serrated-like CRC were predominantly assigned to GINS5.
source: Specifically, serrated-like CRC arising from serrated neoplasia pathway (Marisa et al., 2013), were predominantly assigned to GINS5 and to a lesser extent to other subtypes (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by cellular phenotype analysis, citation, and figure reference

claim: Tumors with the crypt base phenotype were particularly evident for GINS2.
source: Consistently, tumors with the crypt base phenotype were particularly evident for GINS2, whereas other subtypes were mainly concentrated on tumors with the crypt top phenotype, especially GINS6.
evidence: Supported by NTP algorithm analysis

claim: Other subtypes were mainly concentrated on tumors with the crypt top phenotype, especially GINS6.
source: Consistently, tumors with the crypt base phenotype were particularly evident for GINS2, whereas other subtypes were mainly concentrated on tumors with the crypt top phenotype, especially GINS6.
evidence: Supported by NTP algorithm analysis

claim: GINS2 displayed superior stemness abundance relative to other subtypes.
source: Overall, GINS2 displayed superior abundance relative to other subtypes, which was in line with its malignant traits (Figure 8L).
evidence: Supported by stemness signature analysis and figure reference

claim: GINS1 was mainly associated with elevated NOTCH2 and IL13RA2 autocrine stimulation loops.
source: As results, GINS1 was mainly associated with elevated NOTCH2 and IL13RA2 autocrine stimulation loops (Figure 8M and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by SSEA analysis and figure reference

claim: GINS2 displayed high intrinsic TGFBR1 and IGF2R stimulation.
source: GINS2 displayed high intrinsic TGFBR1 and IGF2R stimulation (Figure 8M and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by SSEA analysis and figure reference

claim: GINS3 was characterized by activations of ephrin receptors (EPHA and EPHB signaling).
source: Of note, GINS3 was characterized by activations of ephrin receptors (EPHA and EPHB signaling) (Figure 8M and Figure 8—figure supplement 1), a set of receptors that are activated via binding to Eph receptor interacting proteins and form the largest subfamily of receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs).
evidence: Supported by SSEA analysis and figure reference

claim: GINS3 featured a high EGFR activity.
source: In line with prior findings, GINS3 featured a high EGFR activity (Figure 8M and Figure 8—figure supplement 1), corresponding to its sensitive response to cetuximab.
evidence: Supported by SSEA analysis and figure reference

claim: GINS4 exhibited marked traits of high activities in ACKR2, FGFR1, and IL1R1 stimulation loops.
source: GINS4 exhibited marked traits of high activities in ACKR2, FGFR1, and IL1R1 stimulation loops (Figure 8M and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by SSEA analysis and figure reference

claim: Immune-related autocrine loops including CXCR3, IFNAR1, IFNGR1, TNFRSF9, and TNFRSF10A were attributed to GINS5 tumors.
source: Accordingly, our results attributed immune-related autocrine loops including CXCR3, IFNAR1, IFNGR1, TNFRSF9, and TNFRSF10A to GINS5 tumors (Figure 8M and Figure 8—figure supplement 1), concordant with inflammatory traits of this subtype.
evidence: Supported by SSEA analysis and figure reference

claim: GINS6 was linked to BMP activity.
source: GINS6 was linked to BMP activity (Figure 8M and Figure 8—figure supplement 1), which was reported to restrict stem cell expansion and upregulated at the crypt top with a decreasing gradient towards the crypt base (Kosinski et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by SSEA analysis, figure reference, and citation

claim: PIK3CA mutations were prevalent in GINS1 (45%).
source: PIK3CA mutations could activate PI3K/AKT signaling and further enhance the proliferation and invasion of cancer cells (Raskov et al., 2020), which was prevalent in GINS1 (45%) (Figure 9A).
evidence: Supported by mutation analysis, citation, and figure reference

claim: GINS2 enriched plentiful SMAD4 mutations (53%).
source: GINS2 enriched plentiful SMAD4 mutations (53%), which was strikingly higher than background mutations of SMAD4 in CRC (Raskov et al., 2020; Figure 9A).
evidence: Supported by mutation analysis, citation, and figure reference

claim: KRAS mutations were to a lesser extent in GINS3 (12%).
source: As previously reported, KRAS mutations are widespread in CRC (Raskov et al., 2020), but to a lesser extent in GINS3 (12%) (Figure 9A and Figure 9—figure supplement 1A), in line with its inferior activity of KRAS signaling detected in the discovery cohort.
evidence: Supported by mutation analysis, citation, and figure reference

claim: GINS5 displayed overall rich mutations in driver genes, especially BRAF.
source: GINS5 was previously identified as tumors with high TMB and MSI, and thus displayed overall rich mutations in driver genes (Figure 9A), especially BRAF (Figure 9—figure supplement 1B), which was associated with CRC showing a high level of MSI.
evidence: Supported by mutation analysis and figure reference

claim: GINS5 presented low chromosomal instability (CIN), featured by slight copy number variation (CNV).
source: Conversely, GINS5 presented low chromosomal instability (CIN), featured by slight copy number variation (CNV), whereas an evident CIN phenotype was assigned to GINS3 that possessed heavy CNV burden, including amplifications and deletions (Figure 9A–D).
evidence: Supported by CNV analysis and figure reference

claim: An evident CIN phenotype was assigned to GINS3 that possessed heavy CNV burden.
source: Conversely, GINS5 presented low chromosomal instability (CIN), featured by slight copy number variation (CNV), whereas an evident CIN phenotype was assigned to GINS3 that possessed heavy CNV burden, including amplifications and deletions (Figure 9A–D).
evidence: Supported by CNV analysis and figure reference

claim: The broad amplifications of Chr20 were particularly evident for GINS3.
source: We also observed that the broad amplifications of Chr20 were particularly evident for GINS3 (Figure 9E–F).
evidence: Supported by CNV analysis and figure reference

claim: Tumors with high CIMP were predominantly assigned to GINS5.
source: As previously reported, high CIMP (CIMP-H) was parallel with high MSI (MSI-H)(Raskov et al., 2020), and our results consistently displayed that tumors with MSI-H or CIMP were predominantly assigned to GINS5 (Figure 9G).
evidence: Supported by CIMP analysis, citation, and figure reference

claim: The methylation silencing of SMOC1 was strongly enriched in GINS3.
source: Specifically, the methylation silencing of SMOC1 was strongly enriched in GINS3, and TMEM106A silencing prevalently occurred in GINS4 (Figure 9A).
evidence: Supported by methylation analysis and figure reference

claim: TMEM106A silencing prevalently occurred in GINS4.
source: Specifically, the methylation silencing of SMOC1 was strongly enriched in GINS3, and TMEM106A silencing prevalently occurred in GINS4 (Figure 9A).
evidence: Supported by methylation analysis and figure reference

claim: The expression levels of SMOC1 and TMEM106A were significantly inversely correlated with their methylation levels.
source: The expression levels of these two genes were significantly inversely correlated with their methylation levels (Figure 9H–I).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis and figure reference

claim: Most of GINS2-discriminant genes from the PAM classifier belonged to stromal genes (71.1%).
source: Indeed, most of GINS2-discriminant genes from the PAM classifier belonged to stromal genes (71.1%), followed by GINS4 (47.5%) (Figure 10—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by gene annotation analysis and figure reference

claim: Subtypes with rich stromal components (e.g. GINS2 and GINS4) in human CRC samples were inclined to transform into subtypes with high tumor purity (e.g. GINS1 and GINS3) in corresponding PDX derivatives.
source: In Uronis cohort (chip data)(Uronis et al., 2012) with 27 matched human CRC samples and PDX derivatives, the subtype assignments were incongruent between PDXs and their original counterparts. Subtypes with rich stromal components (e.g. GINS2 and GINS4) in human CRC samples were inclined to transform into subtypes with high tumor purity (e.g. GINS1 and GINS3) in corresponding PDX derivatives (Figure 10B).
evidence: Supported by PDX analysis, citation, and figure reference

claim: Most of the matched post-treatment biopsies after radiotherapy were assigned to GINS2.
source: We observed that the pretreatment specimens were confidently assigned to six subtypes, and most of the matched post-treatment biopsies were assigned to GINS2 (Figure 10D), confirming that stromal component served as the driven factor for GINS2 transitions.
evidence: Supported by radiotherapy response analysis and figure reference

claim: GINS2 displayed a strikingly higher fraction of fibroblasts relative to other subtypes in single cell RNA-seq analysis.
source: GINS2 displayed a strikingly higher fraction of fibroblasts relative to other subtypes (Figure 10—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by single cell RNA-seq analysis and figure reference

claim: GINS2 possessed superior cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAF) score and worse prognosis across all treated samples.
source: As expected, GINS2 possessed superior cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAF) score and worse prognosis across all treated samples (Figure 10—figure supplement 2A-B).
evidence: Supported by CAF score analysis and figure reference

claim: In GINS2 samples, a higher CAF score predicted worse prognosis.
source: Isella et al., 2015 demonstrated that CAF score was a stronger indicator of negative prognosis. In GINS2 samples, a higher CAF score certainly predicted worse prognosis (Figure 10—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by survival analysis, citation, and figure reference

claim: Resistant tumors to radiotherapy were predominantly enriched in GINS2.
source: We also observed that resistant tumors were predominantly enriched in GINS2 (Figure 10—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by radiotherapy response analysis and figure reference

claim: 41 specific-subtype agents were determined for six subtypes.
source: Taking the intersections of two datasets, we determined 41 specific-subtype agents for six subtypes (Figure 10—figure supplement 4 and Supplementary file 14).
evidence: Supported by drug response prediction analysis and figure reference

claim: GINS1-specific drugs include BI-2536, gemcitabine, and paclitaxel that target proliferative pathways.
source: For example, GINS1-specific drugs, BI-2536, gemcitabine, and paclitaxel target proliferative pathways; AZD6482, AZD8055 and temsirolimus target activated PI3K/mTOR signaling arise from PIK3CA mutations, which was strikingly harbored in GINS1; GINS2-specific drugs, linsitinib targets IGF1R signaling and CHIR-99021 targets WNT signaling; six EGFR/RTK signaling inhibitors, afatinib, gefitinib, lapatinib, axitinib, sorafenib, and sunitinib were specifically designed for GINS3; GINS6 featured dysregulated lipid synthesis, which might be targeted by four anticholesterol drugs containing atorvastatin, lovastatin, simvastatin, and fluvastatin.
evidence: Supported by drug-pathway matching analysis

claim: AZD6482, AZD8055 and temsirolimus target activated PI3K/mTOR signaling and are specific for GINS1.
source: For example, GINS1-specific drugs, BI-2536, gemcitabine, and paclitaxel target proliferative pathways; AZD6482, AZD8055 and temsirolimus target activated PI3K/mTOR signaling arise from PIK3CA mutations, which was strikingly harbored in GINS1; GINS2-specific drugs, linsitinib targets IGF1R signaling and CHIR-99021 targets WNT signaling; six EGFR/RTK signaling inhibitors, afatinib, gefitinib, lapatinib, axitinib, sorafenib, and sunitinib were specifically designed for GINS3; GINS6 featured dysregulated lipid synthesis, which might be targeted by four anticholesterol drugs containing atorvastatin, lovastatin, simvastatin, and fluvastatin.
evidence: Supported by drug-pathway matching analysis

source: For example, GINS1-specific drugs, BI-2536, gemcitabine, and paclitaxel target proliferative pathways; AZD6482, AZD8055 and temsirolimus target activated PI3K/mTOR signaling arise from PIK3CA mutations, which was strikingly harbored in GINS1; GINS2-specific drugs, linsitinib targets IGF1R signaling and CHIR-99021 targets WNT signaling; six EGFR/RTK signaling inhibitors, afatinib, gefitinib, lapatinib, axitinib, sorafenib, and sunitinib were specifically designed for GINS3; GINS6 featured dysregulated lipid synthesis, which might be targeted by four anticholesterol drugs containing atorvastatin, lovastatin, simvastatin, and fluvastatin.
evidence: Supported by drug-pathway matching analysis

source: For example, GINS1-specific drugs, BI-2536, gemcitabine, and paclitaxel target proliferative pathways; AZD6482, AZD8055 and temsirolimus target activated PI3K/mTOR signaling arise from PIK3CA mutations, which was strikingly harbored in GINS1; GINS2-specific drugs, linsitinib targets IGF1R signaling and CHIR-99021 targets WNT signaling; six EGFR/RTK signaling inhibitors, afatinib, gefitinib, lapatinib, axitinib, sorafenib, and sunitinib were specifically designed for GINS3; GINS6 featured dysregulated lipid synthesis, which might be targeted by four anticholesterol drugs containing atorvastatin, lovastatin, simvastatin, and fluvastatin.

source: For example, GINS1-specific drugs, BI-2536, gemcitabine, and paclitaxel target proliferative pathways; AZD6482, AZD8055 and temsirolimus target activated PI3K/mTOR signaling arise from PIK3CA mutations, which was strikingly harbored in GINS1; GINS2-specific drugs, linsitinib targets IGF1R signaling and CHIR-99021 targets WNT signaling; six EGFR/RTK signaling inhibitors, afatinib, gefitinib, lapatinib, axitinib, sorafenib, and sunitinib were specifically designed for GINS3; GINS6 featured dysregulated lipid synthesis, which might be targeted by four anticholesterol drugs containing atorvastatin, lovastatin, simvastatin, and fluvastatin.
evidence: Supported by drug-pathway matching analysis

claim: Four PARP inhibitors (olaparib, niraparib, talazoparib, and KU-55933) were specific for GINS5.
source: Notably, we observed that four PARP inhibitors were specific for GINS5, including olaparib, niraparib, talazoparib, and KU-55933 (Figure 10F).
evidence: Supported by drug response prediction analysis and figure reference

claim: Tumors with higher HDR score and mutations were predominantly assigned to GINS5.
source: In the TCGA-CRC cohort, we next compared the HRD score and the proportion of HRD pathway mutations (Liu et al., 2021b) among six subtypes. As expected, tumors with higher HDR score and mutations were predominantly assigned to GINS5 (Figure 10G), suggesting its stronger potential to benefit from PARP inhibitors.
evidence: Supported by HRD analysis, citation, and figure reference

claim: The initial background network from the Reactome database included 6376 genes and 148,942 interactions.
source: The initial background network from the Reactome database (Jassal et al., 2020) included 6376 genes and 148,942 interactions, and fitted the biological scale-free network distribution in the discovery cohort (R=−0.852, p<2.2e-16; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by network construction methodology, citation, and figure reference

claim: The background network fitted the biological scale-free network distribution in the discovery cohort (R=−0.852, p<2.2e-16).
source: The initial background network from the Reactome database (Jassal et al., 2020) included 6376 genes and 148,942 interactions, and fitted the biological scale-free network distribution in the discovery cohort (R=−0.852, p<2.2e-16; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis, citation, and figure reference

claim: Tumor samples displayed remarkably stronger perturbations relative to normal samples (p<2.2e-16).
source: Indeed, tumor samples displayed remarkably stronger perturbations relative to normal samples (p<2.2e-16; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by statistical test and figure reference

claim: 92.6% of all 148,942 gene pairs exhibited more dispersion in tumor samples than in normal samples by comparing the coefficient of variation (CV) of interaction perturbations (P<2.2e-16).
source: Collectively, 92.6% of all 148,942 gene pairs exhibited more dispersion in tumor samples than in normal samples by comparing the coefficient of variation (CV) of interaction perturbations (P<2.2e-16; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figure reference

claim: A total of 6216 patients and 308 normal samples were enrolled from public databases.
source: A total of 6216 patients and 308 normal samples were enrolled from public databases.
evidence: Methodological detail about data sources

claim: 214 clinical CRC samples were enrolled from The First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University for further validation.
source: We also enrolled 214 clinical CRC samples from The First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University for further validation (Supplementary file 3).
